query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal-element alloys (MPEAs) for high‐temperature use, early formation of a coherent, protective oxide scale—primarily consisting of Cr2O3 and/or Al2O3—controls long‐term oxidation resistance and material integrity. The hypothesis posits that when high‐mobility elements such as Mn are minimized or counterbalanced by increased Cr/Al, the alloy rapidly forms and retains a continuous, adherent oxide barrier that limits further oxidation. Conversely, in alloys with higher Mn content, rapid Mn oxidation leads to nonprotective spinels and scale spallation, accelerating oxidation and degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized MPEAs (e.g., equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi or FeNiCuAl-based systems) exhibiting a multiphase microstructure before high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Modifying the alloy composition by reducing the relative content of high-mobility elements (e.g., Mn) and/or increasing the content of protective elements such as Cr and/or Al.
generation.conditions: Prolonged oxidation tests (up to 1000+ hours) conducted in oxygen-rich environments at temperatures ranging from 900 °C to 1200 °C, with controlled oxygen partial pressures.
generation.structural_mediator: The composition, continuity, and interfacial adhesion of the surface oxide scale that forms on the alloy during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: Rapid nucleation and growth of a dense, continuous Cr2O3 and/or Al2O3 scale act as a barrier to inward oxygen diffusion. In alloys with significant Mn, preferential oxidation of Mn leads to the formation of nonprotective spinel oxides, which are prone to spallation and do not prevent further oxidation, thus degrading material integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with reduced Mn content or enhanced Cr/Al levels will form more protective, adherent oxide scales, resulting in slower overall oxide growth, lower mass loss, and improved retention of the base alloy microstructure relative to a baseline MPEA with higher Mn content.
generation.baseline: A standard Ni-based superalloy or an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy with unmodified composition, expected to form nonprotective Mn-rich oxides and exhibit faster oxidation rates under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in the high-temperature oxidation regime of 900–1200 °C and over sustained exposure times (up to 1000+ hours). Its validity outside these temperature and time ranges is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative contributions of individual elemental diffusion kinetics, precise scale nucleation rates, and the interplay between lattice distortion and interfacial chemistry remain uncertain. Further real-time characterization is needed to constrain these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MPEAs: one set with a standard CrMnFeCoNi composition and a second set modified to reduce Mn content while increasing Cr and/or Al. Expose both sets to prolonged oxidation tests in controlled oxygen atmospheres at 900–1200 °C. Utilize time-resolved environmental TEM and synchrotron-based diffraction/tomographic imaging to monitor oxide nucleation, growth, phase evolution, and spallation events.
measurements: Real-time imaging and diffraction to identify and quantify the phases of oxide scales (e.g., Cr2O3, Al2O3 versus Mn-rich spinels)
Measurement of oxide scale thickness and coherence/adherence over time
Mass change measurements to quantify oxidation rate
Elemental diffusion profiles across the oxide/alloy interface using in-situ spectroscopic techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy (with reduced Mn/increased Cr-Al) does not exhibit a significantly more coherent and adherent protective oxide scale, nor a reduced oxidation rate compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis that early formation of a protective oxide scale governs oxidation resistance in these MPEAs is falsified.

decision.trend: Early in-situ X-ray diffraction on CrMnFeCoNi HEAs (2023) revealed that Mn-rich oxides dominated, preventing the formation of more protective phases such as Cr2O3 and leading to substantial mass loss. Subsequent atom probe and electron microscopy studies (2024) showed that oxidation behavior is driven by atomic size, redox potential, and evolving chemical gradients, complicating the stable formation of protective oxides across multiple principal elements. More recently (2026), a NiCoCrAl-based MPEA with tailored microstructure and lattice distortion demonstrated slower oxide growth and enhanced spallation resistance at 1200 °C, indicating that controlling diffusion pathways and ensuring early formation of stable oxide layers can noticeably improve high-temperature oxidation resistance. However, identifying universal mechanisms for stable oxide scale formation and retention across different MPEA compositions and microstructures under prolonged high-temperature exposure remains an open challenge.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in revealing which elements preferentially oxidize first and how altered diffusion paths can help slow oxide growth, the interplay among principal elements that stabilizes a coherent, adherent oxide scale over long durations at 900–1200 °C remains unclear. The thermodynamic and kinetic factors determining whether protective oxides form (e.g., Cr2O3, Al2O3) versus nonprotective oxides (e.g., Mn-rich) are not fully understood, and the role of evolving local composition, lattice distortion, and interfacial chemistry in preventing spallation still needs to be resolved.
decision.lever: Time-resolved environmental TEM or synchrotron-based diffraction/tomographic imaging under varied oxygen partial pressures and temperatures (900–1200°C) for carefully selected MPEAs alongside a well-characterized baseline Ni-based superalloy
decision.why: Real-time observation of oxide nucleation and interfacial evolution will clarify how multi-element synergies drive protective oxide formation and maintain scale cohesiveness. Previous work has identified composition-based effects and diffusion pathways but has not directly monitored how oxide phases form and transition over time in situ. Such experiments can capture the mechanistic details needed to unify current knowledge and guide high-temperature MPEA design strategies.
